newsitem.title: UK: Golf-Indians so impressive on Dunhill debut.
newsitem.headline: Golf-Indians so impressive on Dunhill debut.

text.p: Golfing minnows India won fulsome praise on their Alfred Dunhill Cup debut despite their 2-1 defeat by Zimbabwe.

Though they fell just short of producing a major upset on Thursday against last year's beaten finalists, it was a fine display by three players from a country which has only a handful of courses of championship standard.
"It just goes to show that there is no such thing as an easy match in match play golf," said Tony Johnstone after his 72-73 defeat by Ali Sher in the first of three contests.

After Mark McNulty defeated Asian Masters champion Gaurav Ghei 70-73 -- helped by Ghei's double-bogey six at the 17th where he hit his second into the deep greenside bunker -- Nick Price secured victory by one shot, beating Jeev Singh 70-71.

"I was very impressed. Jeev played really solidly," Price said. "He drove into two bunkers and that cost him the match but they had nothing to lose today. They adopted the attitude that they could just go for it."
McNulty placed India's performance in a wider context when he said world golf had "certainly got better over the past 10 years".
"It doesn't matter where you come from now. If you are playing on any tour -- Asian, Australasian or wherever -- you are obviously a good player.

"I think we have so many more good players in the world now, as opposed to 20 years ago when Americans were dominant. They still are, but there are now really good players from the rest of the world."
Indian team manager Vikramjit Singh said the game was growing rapidly in India.
"We have about 150 courses and, though only four or five are of championship standard, there are new ones being built on designs by Jack Nicklaus, Greg Norman, Arnold Palmer."
Singh said there were around 150 professionals playing on an active Indian circuit and the best players were also doing well on the Omega (Asian) tour.
The Indians failed to qualify for this event four successive times from 1990 to 1993 and were not selected in 1994 and 1995 after qualifying was abolished.
"This is the first time we have been invited and it is a great thrill for us. Playing here is a phenomenal thing for Indian golf," Singh said.
"We are looking to build on this and make our PGA into a more substantial circuit which would create alternative means of making a living for our players."
Ghei, who was taught to play by his father, said he was pleased with his game despite the double-bogey at the 17th, a hole which has wrecked so many hopes over the years.
"I just got into the wrong place at the wrong time," he said. "I had no shot out and could only get on to the road...It's a great hole -- the best par-four in the world."

"We had a good chance of causing a major upset so we are disappointed," said Ghei, whose side can still progress despite losing their first round-robin tie. "We'll give it our best shot. We have no reason to lose heart."
India play defending champions Scotland on Friday and Sweden on Saturday.
